Tafsir (exegesis) of Surat al-Tariq

It is Meccan, and there is no disagreement among the exegetes (mufassirun) on this.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿By the sky and the one who comes by night.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the one who comes by night is?﴾ ﴿It is the piercing star.﴾ ﴿There is no soul but that it has a guardian over it.﴾ ﴿So let man look at what he was created from.﴾ ﴿He was created from a gushing fluid.﴾ ﴿It emerges from between the backbone and the ribs.﴾ ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him.﴾ ﴿On the Day when secrets are examined.﴾ ﴿He will have no power and no helper.﴾

Allah the Exalted swore by the sky, which is well known according to the view of the majority of the exegetes. Some said: here "sky" means rain, and the Arabs call rain "sky" because it comes from the sky, and they also call clouds "sky." The poet said:

"When the sky descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry."

And al-Nabigha said:

"Like the daisy at the morning after its rain-cloud..."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 86, verse 11–17:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿By the sky, which returns [rain]﴾ ﴿and the earth, which splits [open]﴾ ﴿Indeed, it [the Qur'an] is a decisive word﴾ ﴿and it is not a jest﴾ ﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot﴾ ﴿and I am plotting a plot﴾ ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them time, a little while﴾

"Al-sama'" (the sky) in this context may be the well-known sky, and it may be the clouds. "Al-raj'" (return) means the rain and its water, and from it is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"White like the raj', settling when it spreads over an open plain, uprooting [what is in it]."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: "Al-raj' is the clouds and the rain." al-Hasan said: "Because it returns with provision every year." Others said: "Because it returns to the earth." Ibn Zayd said: "Al-raj' is the verbal noun of the return of the sun, the moon and the stars from one state to another, and from it comes manzilah (station), which goes and returns."

"Al-sad'" (splitting) means the plants, because the earth splits open because of them. This view fits the view of those who said that al-raj' is the rain. Mujahid said: "Al-sad' is what is in the earth of ravines, cracks, ditches and fissures made by ploughing and other things; these are matters in which there is a lesson." This view fits the second view regarding "al-raj'".

The pronoun in "innahu" (indeed it) refers to the Qur'an, though it has not been mentioned before, because the discourse concerns a part of it and the context requires it. "Fasl" (decisive) means: decided, the distinguishing of truths from falsehoods. "Al-hazl" (jest) means: vain play.

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed about Quraysh that they plot in their deeds and their words, in their persistent opposition to the Prophet ﷺ, and in their scheming to reject his command. Then Allah the Exalted reinforced that with the verbal noun and emphasized it, and He, glorified be He, informed that He would inflict upon them a punishment which He called a plot, according to the common usage of naming a punishment by the name of the sin. Then it became clear from His saying, "So give respite to the disbelievers," that His punishment for them, which He called a plot, is delayed until it appeared at Badr and elsewhere. Most people recited "amhilhum," and Ibn 'Abbas recited "mahhilhum." In this verse there is a truce which was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

His saying, the Exalted, "ruwaydan" means: a little, as said by Qatadah. This is a circumstantial accusative (hal). When something precedes this word that it describes, as in your saying "sayrun ruwaydan" (a slow march), or when a verb precedes it that governs it, as in this verse, it functions thus. But if you begin with it, saying "Ruwaydan ya fulan" (Slowly, O so-and-so), then it means a command to take one's time, and it operates like the expression "sabran ya Zayd" (patience, O Zayd) and "qalilan ya 'Amr" (a little, O 'Amr).

The commentary of Surah [al-Tariq] is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

﴿By the sky, which returns [rain]﴾ ﴿and the earth, which splits [open]﴾ ﴿Indeed, it [the Qur'an] is a decisive word﴾ ﴿and it is not a jest﴾ ﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot﴾ ﴿and I am plotting a plot﴾ ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them time, a little while﴾

"Al-sama'" (the sky) in this context may be the well-known sky, and it may be the clouds. "Al-raj'" (return) means the rain and its water, and from it is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"White like the raj', settling when it spreads over an open plain, uprooting [what is in it]."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: "Al-raj' is the clouds and the rain." al-Hasan said: "Because it returns with provision every year." Others said: "Because it returns to the earth." Ibn Zayd said: "Al-raj' is the verbal noun of the return of the sun, the moon and the stars from one state to another, and from it comes manzilah (station), which goes and returns."

"Al-sad'" (splitting) means the plants, because the earth splits open because of them. This view fits the view of those who said that al-raj' is the rain. Mujahid said: "Al-sad' is what is in the earth of ravines, cracks, ditches and fissures made by ploughing and other things; these are matters in which there is a lesson." This view fits the second view regarding "al-raj'".

The pronoun in "innahu" (indeed it) refers to the Qur'an, though it has not been mentioned before, because the discourse concerns a part of it and the context requires it. "Fasl" (decisive) means: decided, the distinguishing of truths from falsehoods. "Al-hazl" (jest) means: vain play.

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed about Quraysh that they plot in their deeds and their words, in their persistent opposition to the Prophet ﷺ, and in their scheming to reject his command. Then Allah the Exalted reinforced that with the verbal noun and emphasized it, and He, glorified be He, informed that He would inflict upon them a punishment which He called a plot, according to the common usage of naming a punishment by the name of the sin. Then it became clear from His saying, "So give respite to the disbelievers," that His punishment for them, which He called a plot, is delayed until it appeared at Badr and elsewhere. Most people recited "amhilhum," and Ibn 'Abbas recited "mahhilhum." In this verse there is a truce which was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

His saying, the Exalted, "ruwaydan" means: a little, as said by Qatadah. This is a circumstantial accusative (hal). When something precedes this word that it describes, as in your saying "sayrun ruwaydan" (a slow march), or when a verb precedes it that governs it, as in this verse, it functions thus. But if you begin with it, saying "Ruwaydan ya fulan" (Slowly, O so-and-so), then it means a command to take one's time, and it operates like the expression "sabran ya Zayd" (patience, O Zayd) and "qalilan ya 'Amr" (a little, O 'Amr).

The commentary of Surah [al-Tariq] is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
